_comment: CliniX neurology skills, shared across neurological disease pathways.

skill.hx.neuro.approach.title: Localising from the history alone
skill.hx.neuro.approach.oneLine: Onset, course, and distribution answer WHERE before you touch the patient
skill.hx.neuro.approach.why: In neurology the history often localises the lesion before the examination confirms it. Three questions, onset, course over time, and distribution of the symptom, do most of that work.

asks.text: How did it start: sudden, over hours, over days, or gradually over months?
Has it stayed the same, improved, worsened, or come and gone?
Exactly which part of the body, and does it cross the midline?
Any weakness, numbness, visual change, speech difficulty, or loss of consciousness alongside it?
Headache, and if so, is it the worst of their life or different from their usual pattern?

teach.heading: Onset tells you the mechanism
teach.note: A useful rule of thumb: the faster the onset, the more likely it is vascular; the slower, the more likely it is structural or degenerative.

teach.heading: Course over time is the second axis

points.d: Typical of a vascular event once the initial insult is over.
Recurrent small vascular events, or relapsing demyelination.
A growing structural lesion, or a progressive degenerative process.

teach.heading: Distribution: does it cross the midline
teach.body: A single, well-demarcated body part, or a whole side of the body, suggests a lesion in the central nervous system on the OPPOSITE side. Symptoms that cross the midline, or that follow a specific nerve or root rather than a whole limb, point to the peripheral nervous system instead.

pitfalls: Not asking exactly how fast a symptom developed, which is the single most useful localising question in neurology.
Missing a 'worst headache of my life', which needs subarachnoid haemorrhage actively excluded.

probes.q: A weakness developed over seconds. What category of cause does that suggest?
probes.a: A vascular event, such as a haemorrhage or embolic stroke.

probes.q: Symptoms confined to one whole side of the body. Central or peripheral nervous system?
probes.a: Central, and on the side OPPOSITE the symptoms, because of the crossing of major motor and sensory pathways.

rubric.text: Screens for red-flag headache or sudden severe symptoms

skill.exam.neuro.tone_power.title: Tone and power
skill.exam.neuro.tone_power.oneLine: Two systems, two very different patterns of weakness
skill.exam.neuro.tone_power.why: Tone tells you upper or lower motor neurone before you have finished testing power. Getting this pattern right is what separates a stroke from Guillain-Barre syndrome at the bedside, long before any scan.

steps.text: Assess tone by passively moving each joint through its range, asking the patient to relax.
Test power against a fixed scale (MRC 0 to 5) for each muscle group, comparing both sides.
Test proximal and distal muscles separately in each limb.
Look specifically for a pattern: which limbs, proximal or distal, and symmetry.

skill.exam.neuro.tone_power.normal: Normal tone throughout, power 5/5 in all muscle groups, symmetrical.
skill.exam.neuro.tone_power.abnormal: Increased tone (spasticity or rigidity) or decreased tone (flaccidity), and reduced power in any distribution.
skill.exam.neuro.tone_power.significance: Increased tone with pyramidal-pattern weakness (extensors weaker than flexors in the arm, flexors weaker than extensors in the leg) means an upper motor neurone lesion. Flaccid tone with a glove-and-stocking or focal pattern means a lower motor neurone or peripheral problem.

teach.heading: Upper motor neurone versus lower motor neurone, the whole pattern
teach.note: Learn this as ONE pattern, not five separate facts. A patient either fits the upper motor neurone row across the board or the lower motor neurone row; a mixed picture should make you reconsider the localisation.

teach.heading: Grade power on the MRC scale
points: 1: a flicker of contraction, no movement.
3: movement against gravity, not against resistance.
teach.note: Grade 4 is often subdivided (4-, 4, 4+) in practice, but do not blur 4 and 5. The difference between 'normal' and 'reduced' power matters clinically even when it is subtle.

pitfalls: Testing power without first assessing tone, and so missing the pattern that would have told you where to look.
Not comparing proximal with distal, which is what separates a myopathy from a neuropathy.
Grading power as 'normal' without actually testing against resistance.

probes.q: Spastic tone with an extensor plantar response. Upper or lower motor neurone?
Give the full lower motor neurone pattern: tone, bulk, reflexes, plantar.
probes.a: Reduced tone, wasting, reduced or absent reflexes, and a flexor or absent plantar response.

probes.q: Proximal weakness in both legs, normal reflexes, normal sensation. What category of disease?
probes.a: Likely a myopathy, since proximal, symmetrical weakness with preserved reflexes and sensation is the classic myopathic pattern, unlike the distal pattern typical of most peripheral neuropathies.

rubric.text: Grades power against the MRC scale
Compares proximal with distal and both sides

skill.exam.neuro.reflexes.title: Deep tendon reflexes and the plantar response
skill.exam.neuro.reflexes.oneLine: A reflex arc has two ends; knowing which end is broken localises the lesion
skill.exam.neuro.reflexes.why: A reflex is a simple arc: sensory afferent, spinal segment, motor efferent. An absent or exaggerated reflex tells you which part of that arc, and therefore which level of the nervous system, has failed.

steps.text: Ensure the limb is relaxed and positioned correctly for each reflex.
Strike the tendon briskly with the reflex hammer, letting the hammer fall under its own weight.
Compare both sides for every reflex tested.
If a reflex is absent, reinforce with a distraction manoeuvre (Jendrassik) and try again before calling it truly absent.
Test the plantar response last, stroking the lateral sole firmly with a blunt object.

skill.exam.neuro.reflexes.normal: Symmetrical, present reflexes, a flexor (downgoing) plantar response.
skill.exam.neuro.reflexes.abnormal: Exaggerated, reduced, absent, or asymmetrical reflexes, or an extensor (upgoing) plantar response.
skill.exam.neuro.reflexes.significance: Exaggerated reflexes with an extensor plantar mean an upper motor neurone lesion above the level tested. Absent reflexes mean a lesion of the reflex arc itself, at the nerve, root, or spinal segment level.

teach.heading: The segments, so you can localise
teach.note: A reflex that is absent at one specific level with normal reflexes above and below points precisely at that segment, which is exactly how a single nerve root lesion is localised.

teach.heading: Reading the plantar response correctly
teach.body: Stroke firmly along the lateral border of the sole from heel to the base of the little toe, then curving medially. A normal response is flexion (downgoing) of the great toe. Extension (upgoing), with or without fanning of the other toes, is the Babinski sign.
teach.note: The Babinski sign is present from birth until about 18 months, when the corticospinal tracts myelinate; an extensor response beyond that age is always abnormal and means an upper motor neurone lesion somewhere between the cortex and the spinal segment tested.

pitfalls: Striking too gently, or not letting the hammer fall freely.
Not reinforcing before calling a reflex truly absent.
Confusing withdrawal from a ticklish sole with a genuine plantar response.

probes.q: Which segments does the ankle reflex test?
What is the Babinski sign, and what does it mean in an adult?
probes.a: Extension (upgoing) of the great toe on plantar stimulation, with or without fanning of the other toes. In an adult it always indicates an upper motor neurone lesion.

probes.q: A patient has an absent knee reflex on one side but a normal ankle reflex on the same side. What does that pattern suggest?
probes.a: A lesion affecting specifically the L3/L4 segment or its root on that side, since the reflex arc immediately above and below is intact.

rubric.text: Uses correct hammer technique, letting it fall freely
Compares both sides for every reflex
Reinforces before calling a reflex absent
